questionList.question: Who benefits most from GitHub Copilot Free?

options.text: Enterprises that need audit logs and policy controls
Individuals getting started with Copilot for personal use
Organization admins who need usage reporting
Students or teachers who need Copilot Pro at no cost

questionList.explanation: Copilot Free is designed for individual developers getting started with Copilot for personal use. It provides limited usage and does not include organizational governance features.

questionList.question: Which statement best describes Copilot’s context awareness when generating suggestions?

options.text: Copilot always uses the entire repository history
Copilot considers only the file name and comments
Copilot uses surrounding code, current file contents, and comments to shape suggestions
Copilot only considers public code

questionList.explanation: Inline suggestions primarily use the surrounding code, the current file, comments, and open editor context. Repository-aware Chat in Copilot Enterprise can additionally use indexed repository content.

questionList.question: Does GitHub Copilot guarantee that generated code is always correct and secure?

options.text: Yes, Copilot guarantees security
Yes, Copilot guarantees correctness
No, developers must review and test suggestions
No, but Copilot automatically fixes insecure code

questionList.explanation: Copilot provides non-deterministic suggestions that can be incomplete, incorrect, or insecure. GitHub explicitly expects developers to review, test, lint, scan, and validate outputs. Copilot augments development but offers no guarantee of correctness or security.

questionList.question: Which types of prompts or responses can be blocked by GitHub Copilot's safety filters?

options.text: Hate speech or discriminatory language
Sexually explicit content
Code with logical errors
Strong personal opinions in comments

questionList.explanation: Copilot requests and responses pass through content safety filters designed to block harmful categories such as toxicity (hate/discrimination) and sexually explicit content. These protections target safety and harm, not general code correctness or style.

questionList.question: In VS Code, which built-in action helps you gather logs and diagnostics for Copilot issues?

options.text: GitHub Copilot: Export Telemetry
Developer: Open Runtime Console
GitHub Copilot: Collect Diagnostics
GitHub Copilot: Reset Extension Cache

questionList.explanation: Use the Command Palette action “GitHub Copilot: Collect Diagnostics” to gather environment details and Copilot extension logs for troubleshooting connectivity, auth, or extension behavior in VS Code. This is the standard first step before escalating.

questionList.question: Which of the following is not a valid, current Copilot plan name?

options.text: Copilot Free
Copilot Pro+
Copilot Premium
Copilot Enterprise

questionList.explanation: Official plan names include Copilot Free, Copilot Pro / Pro+ (individual), Copilot Business (organization), and Copilot Enterprise (enterprise). “Copilot Premium” is not an official plan name.

questionList.question: Which platform does not support GitHub Copilot?

options.text: GitHub Enterprise Cloud
GitHub.com
GitHub Enterprise Server (GHES)
Visual Studio Code

questionList.explanation: GitHub documents that Copilot is not available for self-hosted GitHub Enterprise Server (GHES). Copilot is provided as a cloud service for GitHub Enterprise Cloud (GHEC) organizations, GitHub.com, and supported IDEs such as VS Code, Visual Studio, and JetBrains.

questionList.question: Which Copilot admin control limits what content the models can access as input context?

options.text: Code referencing
Content exclusion
Prompt engineering
Telemetry retention

questionList.explanation: Enterprise owners and organization owners can configure content exclusion to prevent selected repositories, directories, file types, or patterns from being used as Copilot context.

questionList.question: When matching public code controls are enabled, about how much surrounding code does Copilot compare to detect matches?

options.text: ~50 characters
~150 characters
~300 characters
The entire file

questionList.explanation: Code referencing checks a suggestion and about 150 characters of surrounding code against public GitHub code to detect close matches. Admins or users can block matched suggestions entirely, or allow them while showing references to the public source for review.

questionList.question: When an enterprise policy enforces a Copilot setting - for example, “block matching public code” - what can organizations do?

options.text: Override it at the organization level
Override it at the repository level
Not override it, enterprise-enforced policies take precedence
Override it for public repos only

questionList.explanation: In GitHub Enterprise Cloud, enterprise-enforced Copilot policies cannot be overridden by organizations or repositories. Lower scopes must comply with enterprise policies. They may apply additional restrictions where supported, but they cannot relax or weaken enterprise-enforced settings.

questionList.question: Is GitHub Copilot available from the command line? If so, what can it help you do?

options.text: No, Copilot is IDE-only
Yes, via Copilot command in the CLI for drafting/explaining commands
Yes, only for Enterprise plans
Yes, if GHES is enabled

questionList.explanation: Copilot CLI brings Copilot to the terminal, helping you draft/explain shell and Git commands, refine flags, and learn usage interactively. Availability depends on your Copilot plan and org policy; GHES is not supported for Copilot.

questionList.question: How does Content exclusion differ from a .gitignore file?

options.text: Both prevent files from being pushed to GitHub
Content exclusion limits what Copilot can use as input context; .gitignore controls what Git tracks
Content exclusion blocks outputs similar to excluded files
.gitignore disables Copilot on ignored files

questionList.explanation: Content exclusion is a Copilot governance control that prevents specified repos/paths/file types/patterns from being used as context. Content exclusion limits what Copilot can use as context.

questionList.question: At which scopes can code referencing / “Suggestions matching public code” be configured?

options.text: Only at the IDE level
At the individual account level and via organization/enterprise policies
Only at the repository level
Only at the enterprise level

questionList.explanation: Code referencing, also called “Suggestions matching public code,” can be configured by individual users or governed through organization and enterprise policies.

questionList.question: If an enterprise policy restricts Copilot to a specific set of AI models/surfaces, what can organizations do?

options.text: Choose any model/surface regardless of enterprise policy
Configure org settings only within the enterprise-allowed set
Override enterprise policy at the repo level
Disable enterprise policy from the org settings page

questionList.explanation: Enterprise owners can enforce or preset Copilot policies (for example, allowed models and surfaces like Chat/Edits/CLI). When enforced, organizations may only configure within the allowed set; repositories inherit and cannot weaken enterprise-level rules.

questionList.question: Which GitHub Copilot capability can autonomously make multi-step code changes and open a pull request for review?

options.text: Copilot Chat inline replies
Copilot coding agent
Content exclusion
Code referencing / matching public code

questionList.explanation: Copilot Edits (Edit mode) assists with user-directed changes, while the Copilot coding agent autonomously performs multi-step tasks and can open a pull request for review.

questionList.question: Which statement about Copilot Knowledge Bases is accurate?

options.text: Available on all Copilot plans
Available on Business and Enterprise
Enterprise-only: use curated docs as chat context on GitHub.com/VS Code
Available on Pro+ and Enterprise

questionList.explanation: Copilot Knowledge Bases are an Enterprise-only capability that lets you curate organization-approved documentation and ground Copilot Chat on GitHub.com and VS Code in those sources for higher-quality answers.

questionList.question: Which targets can be specified in Content exclusion rules?

options.text: Only repositories
Repositories and branches
Repositories, paths/directories, file types, and pattern-based rules
Only file extensions

questionList.explanation: Content exclusion supports multiple target types: entire repositories, specific paths/directories, file types (extensions), and pattern/glob-based selectors. This lets admins draw precise context boundaries without disabling Copilot for the whole codebase.

questionList.question: Which statement best describes repository-aware Copilot Chat on GitHub.com?

options.text: It is available to all plans by default
It’s an Enterprise capability that lets chat reference repository files and documentation on GitHub.com
It runs offline using the IDE only
It requires GHES

questionList.explanation: Copilot Enterprise enables GitHub.com repository-aware Chat, allowing authorized users to reference and reason over repository files and documentation in the browser. This goes beyond IDE-local context and benefits from repository indexing.

questionList.question: In VS Code, where do you enable or disable Copilot inline suggestions globally or per language?

options.text: File → Preferences → Keyboard Shortcuts → GitHub
Settings → Extensions → GitHub Copilot (Inline Suggest: Enable / Enable for [Language])
Source Control → Git → Copilot
Terminal → Integrated → Copilot

questionList.explanation: In VS Code, Copilot’s inline behavior is controlled in Settings → Extensions → GitHub Copilot. You can toggle Inline Suggest: Enable globally and configure inline suggestions on a per-language basis, letting teams keep Copilot active generally while restricting specific stacks.

questionList.question: Where can you find GitHub Copilot extension logs and Electron Developer Tools logs in VS Code?

options.text: Only in GitHub.com → Your profile → Logs
Output panel / Extensions logs folder for Copilot; Developer Tools for Electron logs
Git → Show Git Output (only)
Copilot Chat → /logs command

questionList.explanation: VS Code writes Copilot/extension diagnostics to the Output view and the Extensions logs folder. You can open logs via View → Output → “GitHub Copilot”, and open the extension log files using the Command Palette command “Developer: Open Extension Logs Folder”. Platform-level details live under Developer: Toggle Developer Tools → Console for Electron DevTools.

questionList.question: How do you run “GitHub Copilot: Collect Diagnostics” from the Command Palette in VS Code?

options.text: Ctrl/Cmd+` → type “diagnostics copilot”
View → Explorer → Diagnostics
Ctrl+Shift+P (Windows/Linux) or Cmd+Shift+P (macOS) → type “Collect Diagnostics” → select “GitHub Copilot: Collect Diagnostics”
F1 → “Open Logs” (only)

questionList.explanation: Use the Command Palette (Ctrl+Shift+P on Windows/Linux, Cmd+Shift+P on macOS) and run “GitHub Copilot: Collect Diagnostics.” From the Command Palette, type “Diagnostics” or “Collect Diagnostics”, then select “GitHub Copilot: Collect Diagnostics”. The command packages Copilot logs, environment details, versions, and connectivity information into an editor tab that you can inspect or share with support to help identify connectivity/extension issues.

questionList.question: On which platforms is Copilot Chat available?

options.text: Only VS Code and Visual Studio
GitHub.com, VS Code, Visual Studio, JetBrains IDEs, Eclipse, Xcode, GitHub Mobile, Windows Terminal
Only GitHub.com
Only IDEs (no browser or mobile)

questionList.explanation: GitHub lists multiple surfaces for Copilot Chat, including GitHub.com, major IDEs (Visual Studio Code, Visual Studio, JetBrains IDEs, Eclipse, Xcode), GitHub Mobile, and Windows Terminal. Core chat behavior is similar across these environments, but effective availability still depends on your plan and organization/enterprise policy.

questionList.question: What’s the difference between Copilot Edits – Edit mode and Agent mode?

options.text: Edit = disables approvals; Agent = requires approvals
Edit = user-driven targeted edits; Agent = autonomous multi-step changes (can open a pull requset)
Edit = chat only; Agent = inline only
Edit = repository-aware; Agent = IDE-only

questionList.explanation: Edit mode keeps you in control: you pick files, preview diffs, and accept changes incrementally. It is a user-driven, targeted edit experience where you select the scope, review suggested diffs, and apply or reject changes. Agent mode lets the Copilot coding agent decide which files and commands to run and perform autonomous multi-step work across files and tools, often creating or updating pull requests that you then review and merge.

questionList.question: What do Copilot code reviews and PR summaries provide on GitHub.com?

options.text: Auto-merge PRs
AI review suggestions and natural-language summaries of changes
License scanning
Static code analysis only

questionList.explanation: On GitHub.com, Copilot can generate review suggestions and summaries to accelerate PR understanding. Copilot code review can analyze pull requests and offer inline review comments and suggestions, while Copilot PR summaries generate natural-language overviews of the changes so reviewers can quickly understand scope and intent. These aids do not replace manual mandatory reviews or testing; they help reviewers focus on high-risk areas by condensing diffs and spotting potential issues in the code to be merged.

questionList.question: For individual users, which statement about Copilot access and eligibility is correct?

options.text: Copilot Free is for personal use; Pro is paid but may be free for verified students/teachers/maintainers
Pro is only for organizations
Business is required for single developers
Enterprise includes Pro seats for free

questionList.explanation: Copilot Free is intended for individuals getting started with Copilot and includes limited usage quotas.Copilot Pro (and Pro+) are paid individual subscriptions and Copilot Pro can be free for verified students, teachers, and maintainers of popular open-source projects. You do not need Business or Enterprise plans for a single developer using a personal GitHub account.

questionList.question: Who purchases and assigns seats for Business vs. Enterprise plans?

options.text: Developers purchase directly in the IDE
Org owners purchase/assign Business; Enterprise owners manage Enterprise subscriptions and seat assignment
Repository admins purchase both
Students purchase Enterprise

questionList.explanation: For Copilot Business, organization owners subscribe at the organization level, purchase Copilot seats, and assign them to organization members. For Copilot Enterprise, enterprise owners subscribe at the enterprise layer and centrally manage plans and seat assignment across organizations, delegating as needed while respecting organization boundaries.

questionList.question: Which answer best captures the Copilot plan taxonomy and key highlights?

options.text: Free, Team, Premium
Free / Pro (individual), Pro+ (individual), Business (org), Enterprise (org)
Pro, Business, Enterprise only
Free, Team, Enterprise Server

questionList.explanation: GitHub’s current plan taxonomy distinguishes individual plans (Copilot Free, Copilot Pro, Copilot Pro+) and organization/enterprise plans (Copilot Business, Copilot Enterprise). As you move up tiers, you gain governance and policy controls (such as usage reporting and content exclusion) and enterprise capabilities (such as, SSO integrations, audit logs, repo-aware chat, and advanced data controls).

questionList.question: What’s the practical contrast in how developers invoke Copilot features?

options.text: Inline suggestions: appear near the cursor (accept with Tab/Enter). Chat: open a chat panel and prompt (supports selections).
Both are automatically applied without user action
Only chat can generate code; inline cannot
Inline runs in the browser; chat runs only in IDEs

questionList.explanation: Inline is a lightweight completion experience that appears as ghost text near the cursor and is accepted via keys such as Tab/Enter. Chat is invoked by opening a chat view or inline chat, then typing prompts that can use selected code or files as context. Both experiences run in supported IDEs, while Copilot Chat is also available on GitHub.com and Windows Terminal.

questionList.question: Can Copilot help generate unit tests in supported IDEs?

options.text: No, only refactors are supported
Yes, use Copilot Chat or context prompts to generate tests for selected code
Only on Enterprise plans
Only in JetBrains IDEs

questionList.explanation: Copilot Chat and prompt patterns support test generation for selected code. In supported IDEs you can select a function or file and ask Copilot to generate unit (or integration) tests, and Copilot will propose test cases, scaffolds, and assertions based on the surrounding context. Guides such as “Writing tests with GitHub Copilot” also describe using prompts or command ( /tests) to generate tests.

questionList.question: Is Windows Terminal a supported surface for Copilot Chat?

options.text: No, terminal isn’t supported
Yes, Windows Terminal is listed among supported Copilot Chat surfaces
Yes, but only on GHES
Only if you disable inline suggestions

questionList.explanation: GitHub includes Windows Terminal among the supported surfaces for Copilot Chat. With Terminal Chat in Windows Terminal, you can ask Copilot for command suggestions, explanations directly in the terminal.

questionList.question: How can Copilot help with documentation tasks such as docstrings, README sections, and code comments?

options.text: It can only generate code, not docs
Use Copilot Chat and selection-based prompts to draft docstrings, comments, and README snippets
Docs are generated automatically on every commit
Only Enterprise plans can generate documentation

questionList.explanation: Copilot supports documentation workflows. You can select code and ask Copilot Chat to “write docstrings,” “explain this function,” or “draft a README section”. Inline suggestions also surface comment completions near the cursor.

questionList.question: How can Copilot assist with debugging and fixing errors?

options.text: It automatically fixes all errors at build time
Use Copilot Chat to explain error messages/stack traces and propose fixes or refactors
Errors must be fixed manually; Copilot doesn’t help
Only Enterprise users can use Chat for debugging

questionList.explanation: Copilot Chat can analyze error messages, stack traces, and selected code, then propose root cause hypotheses, fixes, and refactors. You can paste error messages or stack traces into Chat, or invoke Copilot from debugging contexts, and ask it to explain the error, identify likely causes, and propose code changes.

questionList.question: How can Copilot support a TDD (Red→Green→Refactor) workflow?

options.text: By generating test scaffolds/cases from selections and then helping refactor after tests pass
By auto-approving PRs when tests pass
By disabling tests during development
By replacing the need for assertions

questionList.explanation: Use Copilot Chat to generate tests from a selected function or acceptance criteria for the red stage, where tests initially fail. Then iterate on the implementation with inline suggestions or Copilot Edits until the tests pass, the green stage. After that, ask Copilot to propose refactors that preserve behavior while tests guard against regressions, the refactor stage.

questionList.question: What actually happens when you accept an inline suggestion?

options.text: The suggestion is inserted into your editor; you decide whether to keep, edit, or discard
The code is auto-committed and pushed
The change is merged to main if CI passes
An audit log entry is always generated

questionList.explanation: Inline suggestions appear near the cursor as ghost text and are accepted via Tab/Enter or editor-specific key bindings. When you accept an inline suggestion, the ghost text becomes real code in your editor, just as if you had typed it yourself. The code is not automatically staged, committed, or pushed, and there is no auto-merge. You retain full control over further edits, staging, commits, and pushes through your normal Git workflow.

questionList.question: How can Copilot help you understand an unfamiliar file or component in your codebase?

options.text: Only repository-aware chat in Enterprise can explain files
It can’t, Copilot only writes code
Use selection/file prompts in Copilot Chat to summarize purpose, dependencies, and risks
You must upload files to a third-party site

questionList.explanation: In supported IDEs, you can select a file or key regions of code and ask Copilot Chat to summarize the purpose, describe dependencies, and highlight potential risks or edge cases.

questionList.question: Which is the best-crafted prompt?

options.text: Write a function to reverse a string
Function in code to reverse a string
Suggest some code to reverse a string
Write a Python function to reverse a string using slicing

questionList.explanation: Effective prompts specify language, task, and method/constraints. Stating “Python” + “reverse a string” + “using slicing” removes ambiguity and guides the model to the intended pattern. A well-crafted prompt usually names the language, the action, the object, and any key constraint in a single concise sentence, so Copilot does less guessing and more targeted completion.

questionList.question: How do you improve ambiguous prompts?

options.text: Use shorter prompts
Avoid specifying language
Retry without changes
Provide more context and details

questionList.explanation: Ambiguous prompts force the model to guess. Adding specific context (file or selection, domain facts), clear intent (what to build or change), and constraints (language, framework, format, performance or style requirements) reliably improves accuracy. Define inputs/outputs and minimal acceptance criteria so the model follows instead of guessing, matching the guidance to avoid ambiguity by adding project context, clear goals, and specific requirements.

questionList.question: Which technique most reliably boosts output quality?

options.text: Use detailed instructions with examples
Use vague prompts
Avoid comments in code
Skip specifying input or output

questionList.explanation: Use detailed instructions with small, concrete examples anchors the format, tone, and structure the model should match, reducing guesswork. The prompt-engineering guidance explicitly encourages “give examples” so Copilot can see the pattern you want and apply it to new cases, instead of inventing style and structure on its own.

questionList.question: Why does adding examples help?

options.text: Examples distract the AI
They reduce Copilot’s ability to generate code
They slow completions
They align output with the desired style/pattern

questionList.explanation: Short few-shot examples show the model the shape you want (naming, layout, docstrings, tests), so generated output conforms to your pattern. Examples effectively shows, not tell the desired style, structure, and tone, which is why prompt-engineering guidance recommends “give examples” so Copilot can generalize from patterns instead of guessing.

questionList.question: Why is context crucial in prompts?

options.text: It consumes more tokens
It helps Copilot generate relevant and accurate suggestions
It prevents completions
It reduces security

questionList.explanation: Copilot conditions on the surrounding code, the current file, and your prompt. Because Copilot does prediction, not execution, the closer and richer the context around the prompt, the more relevant and accurate the suggestions. Prompts that reference the right file/selection, types, interfaces, and data shapes give Copilot a much clearer target than generic requests.

questionList.question: What should you do if Copilot generates irrelevant suggestions?

options.text: Stop using Copilot
Refine or rephrase the prompt with more context
Use shorter prompts
Disable duplication detection

questionList.explanation: Irrelevance usually means missing or misaligned output. Instead of giving up or just retrying, you improve quality by refining the prompt with more context and clearer intent: add a selection/file, specify inputs/outputs, name the language/tooling, and set constraints so Copilot has less room to guess.

questionList.question: Which practice helps Copilot match project style?

options.text: Avoid adding comments
Use vague instructions
Skip output format
Add snippets and style examples

questionList.explanation: Supplying snippets and style examples (naming, error handling, test layout, docstrings) guides Copilot to mirror your project’s conventions. Prompt-engineering guidance explicitly recommends providing project-specific examples so Copilot can follow your patterns instead of inventing its own style.

questionList.question: Which statement best describes what Copilot relies on during inference?

options.text: Runtime execution of your code
Your prompts, file contents, and surrounding code context
Web searches via Bing
Pre-stored templates

questionList.explanation: Copilot performs contextual prediction, not execution. It uses your prompt, the current file and surrounding code, and other allowed context (for example, chat history or repo index) to generate suggestions. It does not run your program or call external web search at inference time; quality depends on how good the available context is.

questionList.question: What does content exclusion let organizations do and why is it relevant to prompting?

options.text: Speed up Copilot
Disable Copilot entirely
Publish private code
Prevent specified repos/paths/file types/patterns from being used as input context

questionList.explanation: Content exclusion lets organizations with Copilot Business or Enterprise define what input context Copilot can see. Admins can exclude specific repositories, directories/paths, file types, or pattern-based rules, preventing that content from being used as context for suggestions in IDEs and on GitHub.com, even if users prompt near it. This keeps secrets and sensitive code and intellectual property out of Copilot’s prompt context.

questionList.question: Which Copilot plans include content exclusion?

options.text: Free and Individual
Business and Enterprise
Individual only
Free only

questionList.explanation: Content exclusion is an organization-level control available on Copilot Business and Copilot Enterprise. It lets organization and enterprise admins define which repositories, directories/paths, file types, or patterns Copilot can use as input context in IDEs and on GitHub.com.

questionList.question: Which prompt gives Copilot the clearest output target?

options.text: “Summarize this.”
“Summarize this function in 3 bullets for junior devs; include inputs, outputs, and one caveat.”
“Explain code.”
“Write notes.”

questionList.explanation: Stating the audience, length/structure, and must-include items creates a concrete target. A prompt like “summarize this function in 3 bullets for junior devs; include inputs, outputs, and one caveat” defines format (bullets), length (3), audience (junior devs), and required content (inputs/outputs/caveat), so Copilot has a very clear output shape and less room to guess.

questionList.question: When asking Copilot to refactor code, which prompt is best?

options.text: “Improve this.”
“Make it cleaner.”
“Rewrite completely.”
“Refactor to pure functions; no side effects; keep same public API; add docstrings; return early on invalid input.”

questionList.explanation: Refactor prompts work best when constraints are explicit: style (pure functions, no side effects), compatibility (keep the same public API and behavior), non-functional requirements (add docstrings), and guardrails (return early on invalid input). This matches refactoring guidance that structure should change but observable behavior must remain the same and tests should continue to pass.

questionList.question: Which prompt best reduces hallucinations when generating API code?

options.text: “Use the Foo API.”
“Use Foo API v3; only endpoints /users/{id}, /users/search; TypeScript; fetch; no undocumented fields; include error handling for 4xx/5xx.”
“Write users code.”
“Guess the latest endpoints.”

questionList.explanation: Hallucinations drop when you fix the API version, restrict which endpoints can be used, and specify language and tooling. A prompt like “Use Foo API v3; only endpoints /users/{id}, /users/search; TypeScript; fetch; no undocumented fields; include error handling for 4xx/5xx” defines a constrained, testable contract instead of an open-ended request, and “no undocumented fields” explicitly discourages Copilot from inventing properties or methods.

questionList.question: You want table-driven unit tests. Which prompt is best?

options.text: “Generate table-driven tests in Go for Parse(), covering empty, invalid, edge lengths; include names and wantErr.”
“Write table-driven tests.”
“Test everything table-driven.”
“Add some asserts for table-driven test.”

questionList.explanation: Specifying language (Go), test style (“table-driven tests”), the target function (Parse()), and cases/fields (“covering empty, invalid, edge lengths; include names and wantErr”) gives Copilot a concrete, idiomatic template to expand. This matches common Go patterns where tests use a []struct{ name string; input …; want …; wantErr bool } table and iterate over named cases.

questionList.question: Which prompt provides the most effective context for generating a robust SQL query?

options.text: “PostgreSQL 14; given schema (tables/columns below); return top 5 customers by revenue last 30 days; output columns: id, name, revenue.”
“Given schema (tables/columns below); return top 5 customers by revenue last 30 days; include window fn for rank; output columns: id, name, revenue, rank.”
“Write a SQL query using the schema below to return the top 5 customers by revenue in the last 30 days; choose any appropriate columns.”
“PostgreSQL 14; given schema (tables/columns below); return top 5 customers by revenue last 30 days; include window fn for rank; output columns: id, name, revenue, rank.”

questionList.explanation: Pinning dialect/version, schema, time window, and required columns steers Copilot away from generic or wrong SQL and toward a verifiable, project-ready query. High-quality SQL prompts should explicitly name the SQL dialect and version, provide the relevant tables/columns, describe the business question and filters, and specify the output shape and ordering, so Copilot generates syntactically correct, planner-friendly SQL for that engine instead of generic guesses.

questionList.question: Which prompt best directs Copilot to produce safe code for secrets?

options.text: “Use an API key from an environment variable; if it’s missing, fall back to a default test key and log the value for debugging.”
“Get the API key from a secrets manager or environment variable; if unavailable, continue with limited functionality and log configuration details.”
“Read API key from env var; do not hardcode; fail fast if missing; log-safe (no secrets in logs); show minimal example.”
“Store the API key in a configuration file checked into the repo; document that it should not be shared publicly.”

questionList.explanation: Security-sensitive prompts should forbid hardcoding, require environment-based or secret-manager configuration, and mandate safe logging and fail-fast behavior if configuration is missing. A prompt like “read API key from env var; do not hardcode; fail fast if missing; log-safe (no secrets in logs)” turns security rules into explicit constraints so Copilot proposes patterns that align with secure coding practices instead of convenient but unsafe shortcuts.

questionList.question: You want Copilot to explain a complex file to a new teammate. Which prompt is best?

options.text: “Explain this file in detail: what it does, how it works, and any important parts.”
“Summarize this file for engineers: main purpose, data flows, and dependencies.”
“Create a thorough explanation of this file, including architecture, flows, and risks, with no strict length limit.”
“Explain this file for a new backend hire: purpose, key data flows, external dependencies, risks; 5 bullets max.”

questionList.explanation: Defining the audience, sections and length focuses the explanation on onboarding value rather than arbitrary detail. A prompt like “explain this file for a new backend hire: purpose, key data flows, external dependencies, risks; 5 bullets max” tells Copilot who the explanation is for, which topics to cover, and how concise to be, ensuring the result is structured, skimmable, and useful for ramp-up.

questionList.question: Which prompt targets a performance-aware implementation?

options.text: “Write a streaming JSON parser in Node.js; O(1) extra space; handle 10MB+ inputs; backpressure with streams; include benchmarks stub.”
“Write a streaming JSON parser in Node.js that can handle 10MB+ inputs and include a simple benchmark.”
“Write a fast JSON parser in Node.js; it should parse 10MB+ inputs and be efficient.”
“Write a JSON parser in any language; prioritize performance and document how to test its speed.”

questionList.explanation: Performance prompts must specify the language/runtime, space/time constraints, workload size, and internal mechanisms (such as streaming and backpressure) to avoid naive, all-in-memory solutions. A prompt like “Write a streaming JSON parser in Node.js; O(1) extra space; handle 10MB+ inputs; backpressure with streams; include benchmarks stub” locks down constraints so Copilot targets a production-grade implementation.

questionList.question: Which prompt best constrains the output format so it can be pasted cleanly into a CI pipeline?

options.text: “List failing tests with their names and error messages in any readable format.”
“Output JSON array of failing tests with fields: name, file, line, message; no prose.”
“Return failing tests as JSON with test name and message, plus a short explanation of likely causes.”
“Output a human-readable report of failing tests, grouped by file, suitable for pasting into chat or email.”

questionList.explanation: Specifying a explicit serialization format, the exact schema fields, and forbidding extra conversational prose yields machine-consumable output that scripts can parse without post-processing. Stripping prose ensures that automated systems do not run into parsing issues due to unstructured introduction or conclusion sentences.

questionList.question: You need an ordered migration plan before any code is generated. Which prompt is best?

options.text: “Create a short plan to migrate this service from Flask to FastAPI, focusing on the main steps required to complete the migration.”
“Outline the tasks to move this service from Flask to FastAPI and then implement the new routes in FastAPI.”
“Create a 5-step plan to migrate Flask → FastAPI; list risks, roll-back steps, and how to keep routes backward-compatible.”
“Provide FastAPI code that replicates the current Flask service’s behavior, assuming breaking changes are acceptable if they simplify the migration.”

questionList.explanation: Requesting a short, ordered plan with risks and backward-compatibility constraints clarifies architectural choices before jumping into code. A prompt like “Create a 5-step plan to migrate Flask → FastAPI; list risks, roll-back steps, and how to keep routes backward-compatible” isolates planning from execution and forces risk assessment early.

questionList.question: Which prompt reduces overbroad refactors in large files?

options.text: “Refactor the parseHeader logic to make it clearer and more robust across the parser code.”
“Update the parser to handle invalid headers better and improve error messages throughout the file.”
“Tidy up parseHeader and related helpers, improving structure and naming wherever it seems useful.”
“Modify only function parseHeader; keep public behavior; add bounds checks; return detailed errors.”

questionList.explanation: Limiting the edit scope to a single named function, maintaining behavioral contracts, and listing specific modifications prevents Copilot from tweaking unrelated logic across a large file. This focuses Copilot’s editing window precisely on the target code block.

questionList.question: How do you best prompt Copilot for secure and resilient HTTP handling?

options.text: “Use HTTPS; validate TLS certs; set timeouts and retries; redact secrets in logs; handle 429/5xx with backoff.”
“Call the API over HTTPS and log the full request and response body for debugging if something goes wrong.”
“Use HTTPS with a reasonable timeout and retry a few times on failure.”
“Call the API with HTTPS but skip strict certificate validation to avoid connection issues.”

questionList.explanation: Security and reliability require explicit constraints: clear protocol verification (TLS validation), explicit timeouts, backoff retry handling for specific response codes, and credential redactions. This ensures Copilot doesn't introduce default, fragile connection boilerplate.

questionList.question: Which prompt best avoids unsupported or hallucinated library calls?

options.text: “Use Redis with a standard client library and configure basic connection settings for your environment.”
“Initialize Redis in Python using redis-py and show how to set and get a key for caching.”
“Use Redis for caching in your service and choose any compatible client version that works with your stack.”
“Python 3.11; redis-py v5 only; use Redis.from_url; no deprecated APIs; include connection timeout and health check.”

questionList.explanation: Pinning the runtime language version, the exact library major/minor version, and specifying allowed constructor targets drastically cuts down on legacy or deprecated API usage. It ensures the boilerplate aligns strictly with your project environment's real dependencies.

questionList.question: What is the best way to prompt for a highly predictable CLI tool?

options.text: “Create a Python CLI with argparse; flags: --input, --format (json|csv), --verbose; validate files; exit codes 0/2; examples.”
“Write a Python CLI that accepts some arguments and prints a result based on the input.”
“Create a CLI script in any language that processes an input file and prints output to the console.”
“Set up a simple command-line entry point without worrying about validation, exit codes, or detailed help text.”

questionList.explanation: Explicitly noting the parser library (argparse), enumerating flags, restricting parameter choices, and specifying semantic system exit codes ensures Copilot builds standard, Unix-compliant tools without making arbitrary architectural guesses.

questionList.question: Which prompt best demonstrates how to execute a safe database migration?

options.text: “Add a new status column and update the application to start using it, then remove old fields later if needed.”
“Update the schema and data to support a status field in a way that works for your database engine.”
“Add column status (ENUM) with default ‘new’; backfill from state; online migration (no downtime); include rollback SQL.”
“Redesign the schema to better model status and deploy the changes during a low-traffic window, accepting some downtime.”

questionList.explanation: Migrations need exact DDL, backfill rules, an online strategy (no downtime), and a clear rollback path so changes can ship safely without blocking deploys or corrupting data. A prompt like “Add column status (ENUM) with default ‘new’; backfill from state; online migration (no downtime); include rollback SQL” describes the schema change, how to derive values from existing data, and how to roll back if needed.

questionList.question: Which prompt best constrains logging for privacy?

options.text: “Add JSON logs with level and message, and include full request and response bodies to simplify debugging.”
“Add structured logs with level, event, and user details; include tokens in debug mode to help trace issues.”
“Add structured JSON logs: level, event, requestId; no PII; redact tokens; include error stack; single line per event.”
“Enable verbose logging across the service, capturing all available fields by default and filtering sensitive data later if needed.”

questionList.explanation: Privacy-aware logging specifies structure, fields, and redaction rules so logs stay machine-parsable and do not leak secrets or PII. A prompt like “Add structured JSON logs: level, event, requestId; no PII; redact tokens; include error stack; single line per event” defines the log schema, correlation IDs, redaction behavior, and one-event-per-line constraint.

questionList.question: Which plan offers enterprise proxy support and integration with advanced compliance capabilities?

options.text: Copilot Free, for individuals without governance or compliance controls
Copilot Individual (Pro/Pro+), with premium personal features only
Copilot Enterprise
Copilot Business, with org-level license management and policies but not full enterprise compliance integrations

questionList.explanation: Copilot Enterprise is the enterprise-tier plan for GitHub Enterprise Cloud organizations. It includes all Copilot Business capabilities (centralized management, org policies, content exclusion, Copilot audit logs) and adds enterprise-grade features such as deeper integration with enterprise identity and governance, advanced compliance support, and enterprise-level network controls like subscription-based routing and proxy/allowlisting configuration at the enterprise scope.

questionList.question: Which plan provides organizational license management and usage reporting without advanced enterprise compliance integrations?

options.text: Copilot Free
Copilot Individual Pro
Copilot Individual Pro+
Copilot Enterprise

questionList.explanation: Copilot Enterprise is designed for GitHub Enterprise Cloud customers who need advanced compliance and governance on top of org-level controls. It includes all Copilot Business capabilities (centralized license management, policies, content exclusion, and Copilot audit logs) and adds enterprise-grade features such as deeper integration with enterprise identity and governance, advanced compliance support, and enterprise-level network controls like proxy/allowlisting and network routing.

questionList.question: What’s the practical difference between Copilot Edits – Edit mode and Agent mode?

options.text: Edit auto-merges; Agent requires reviews
Edit = user-scoped diffs; Agent = autonomous, multi-step execution that may culminate in a PR
Edit is IDE-only; Agent is GitHub.com only
Edit reads the repo; Agent can’t

questionList.explanation: With Copilot Edits – Edit mode, you keep tight control: you pick which files Copilot may change, review the proposed diffs, and apply them incrementally. With Agent mode, Copilot can plan and execute a multi-step workflow—it can inspect the broader project, choose relevant files, run tools or commands, and iterate until the task is complete. The practical difference is scope and autonomy: Edit mode is user-scoped diffs, while Agent mode is autonomous orchestration across files and tools, which in practice often feeds into changes that eventually end up in a pull request for review.

questionList.question: Which plan provides organizational license management and usage reporting without enterprise integrations (like audit logs/SSO)?

options.text: Copilot Free
Copilot Individual Pro
Copilot Business
Copilot Individual Pro+

questionList.explanation: Copilot Business is the first plan that provides organization-level license management and usage reporting, along with policy controls such as content exclusion. Organization and enterprise owners on Business can assign Copilot seats, download detailed activity and usage reports, and configure policies for their members. Copilot Enterprise includes all of these capabilities and adds deeper enterprise-grade integrations for identity, compliance, and governance.

questionList.question: Which of the following is a primary developer use case for Copilot?

options.text: Helping explore unfamiliar APIs and libraries
Automating end-to-end payroll and compliance processing for HR teams
Drafting legally binding corporate contracts without human review
Managing calendar invites, meeting rooms, and company-wide scheduling

questionList.explanation: GitHub Copilot and Copilot Chat are designed to act as an AI pair programmer, helping you understand and use new APIs and libraries by generating example calls, scaffolding common patterns, and explaining code and errors in natural language. When working with an unfamiliar SDK or framework, you can ask Copilot Chat to propose usage examples, explain parameters, and even generate tests, turning exploration of new APIs into an iterative, guided workflow.

questionList.question: Which setting governs similar-but-not-exact suggestions that resemble public code?

options.text: Content exclusion
Code referencing (matching public code)
Duplication-detection filter
Usage reporting

questionList.explanation: Code referencing is the mechanism Copilot uses when you allow suggestions that match or resemble public code. The policy for suggestions that match public code can be set to block these suggestions entirely, or allow them and show references, in which case Copilot surfaces links to the public repositories where similar code was found. This setting governs how Copilot handles similar-but-not-exact public-code matches, whereas content exclusion only controls which inputs Copilot can see.

questionList.question: When code referencing is set to “Allow + show references”, what should you expect?

options.text: Copilot blocks all similar suggestions
Copilot may show the suggestion with links to public sources
Duplication filter is disabled
Content exclusion is ignored

questionList.explanation: When code referencing is configured to “Allow + show references”, Copilot can surface suggestions that match or resemble public code and attach references to public repositories where similar code appears. This lets developers review the origin of the code and make informed decisions about attribution and licensing before accepting the suggestion.

questionList.question: At what scopes can you configure code referencing behavior?

options.text: Only repository level
Individual account and org/enterprise policies
Only enterprise level
Only IDE settings

questionList.explanation: Code referencing and related “suggestions matching public code” behavior are controlled by policies at multiple scopes. As an individual, you can configure whether to block suggestions that match public code or allow + show references, unless your setting is overridden by your organization or enterprise. Organization and enterprise owners can define policies that apply to all users who receive Copilot seats through them, and these higher-level policies take precedence over individual preferences.

questionList.question: Which roles can manage content exclusion policies?

options.text: Outside collaborators only
People with Maintain role
Repository administrators, organization owners, and enterprise owners
Any repository contributor

questionList.explanation: Content exclusion is an administrative control. GitHub Docs state that repository administrators, organization owners, and enterprise owners can manage content exclusion settings, while users with the Maintain role can only view the configuration for a repository and cannot edit it. Outside collaborators and general contributors do not have permission to change content exclusion settings.
